📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s a upcoming way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!

According to recent reports, designer Michael Flarup has just debuted a fresh Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.

In a recent development, doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.

Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!).

Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.).

Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.

There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.

Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.

Industry observers note that he had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.

Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.

Recent findings suggest that “The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup noted.

That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, upcoming things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.

According to recent reports, “That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.

The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
  • The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported.
  • Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

It has been revealed that right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Newly introduced York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It has been revealed that it’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

Industry observers note that the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the fresh pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its users.

In a recent development, given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

It has been revealed that finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

The Delivery Protection Act is at the moment stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly notes “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font revision.” Additionally:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CEO Elon Musk mentioned SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk stated, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

In a recent development, “We’ve got a proposal that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”.

In a recent development, the company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with prepares to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Industry observers note that combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he mentioned. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”.

Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”.

The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell remarked during the firm’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

According to recent reports, even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

SpaceX’s initiative to build a hybrid celluar-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

“I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he noted, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”.

The GTA 6 star system claims a lot more than just your Wanted level

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockstar Games' first gameplay trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 from August suggested the developer had tinkered with some of the core mechanics of the series, including Wanted levels.
  • Recent findings suggest that some of this is thanks to the game's fresh concept of Heat, pieces of information the police learn about the player characters that can linger even after your Wanted level lowers.
  • The most obvious visual difference between GTA 6 and GTA 5 is the reintroduction of a sixth Wanted level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games' first gameplay trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 from August suggested the developer had tinkered with some of the core mechanics of the series, including Wanted levels. Now that GTA 6 is out, we have a much better sense of how much has actually changed. While your Wanted level has always been able to communicate a sense of how many police officers are looking for you and how intently they're looking, the updated system also bakes in a lot more detail about what police actively know about protagonists Jason and Lucia.

Recent findings suggest that some of this is thanks to the game's fresh concept of Heat, pieces of information the police learn about the player characters that can linger even after your Wanted level lowers. But the visual changes to the Wanted system's iconic star ratings convey nearly as much. Here's how Rockstar's approach to Wanted levels has changed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

The most obvious visual difference between GTA 6 and GTA 5 is the reintroduction of a sixth Wanted level. In the last Grand Theft Auto, your Wanted level maxed out at five stars. As Rockstar teased during its gameplay trailer, GTA 6 caps out at six stars. This is a return to the rating system of older games, going as far back as Grand Theft Auto III — or even further if you consider the "police heads" top-down GTA games used to communicate police response.

Recent findings suggest that as in past games, the number of stars lets you know how hard the police are looking for you. One star could just be a few cops tailing you, while a full six stars indicates a dramatic, militarized response. Besides being a throwback, opting for six stars seems like it allows Rockstar to offer some nuance and variety to the series' classic chase experience. You might eventually get bored if every bank robbery devolves into a helicopter chase.

In a recent development, just committing a robbery doesn't necessarily mean your Wanted level will rise, either. According to IGN's hands-on demo and interview with Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson, crimes need to actually be reported to police to provoke a response. "The Wanted system in GTA 6 requires that someone witness the crime, or an alarm needs to be set off for it to be reported to the law," Nelson told IGN. "Our dispatch is extremely specific in what it knows.".

Recent findings suggest that once you are "wanted" for a crime, GTA 6 offers a lot more visual information to tell you what police presently know and nudge you toward escaping their scrutiny. Those include icons for the different kinds of information the police know about you as part of the Heat system, and also different treatments of your Wanted level star rating.

According to recent reports, when police have direct line of sight with you, your stars are solid white, according to GameSpot, and only start flashing white once you've broken line of sight. Meanwhile, your stars turn red when you're near a crime scene but the police don't know where you are or hollow white when the police are looking for you but have no idea what you look like.

Sources indicate that at the same time, some information about the police is also obstructed. GameSpot reports you won't be able to see the police on your minimap, which makes it harder to initiative escape routes in advance. It also states once you do reach a six-star Wanted level, you'll be pursued throughout the game map, making clean exits more difficult. All of these changes seem like they'll make the fundamental cops-and-robbers gameplay of Grand Theft Auto 6 more engaging. Or at the very least, different from what people have come to expect from the series.

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An key note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#1442. Latest Update: GTA 6 fans are flying planes into buildings (or trying to)

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (801 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: GTA 6 fans are flying planes into buildings (or trying to)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) launched on Nov.
  • The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction.
  • In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) launched on Nov. 19, prompting gamers everywhere to take the day off and indulge in a lawless land of hedonism and crime. Unsurprisingly, one of the first activities some people tried in the open world sandbox game was to fly a plane into a building. However, these antics haven't been producing the results many expected.

The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction. Even so, there is particular sensitivity around the subject of crashing planes into buildings. The 9/11 attacks 25 years ago remain a pivotal moment in the U.S. consciousness, to such an extent that many people's minds immediately venture there when presented with a plane and a building.

In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact. Previous Grand Theft Auto games also didn't allow planes to damage buildings. Nevertheless, some fans wondered if GTA 6 would skew this trend, particularly as it aims to feel realistic.

According to early gameplay clips, this doesn't seem to be the case. In a widely circulated clip by Twitch streamer Windpress, his character parachutes from a plane aimed at a building, only to watch the aircraft apparently pass harmlessly through it. Another popular GTA 6 gameplay video from @DiegoPalmaX revealed a manned plane collide with a building but remain completely intact, slowly falling to the ground and even hitting another structure on the way down.

Such clips have drawn criticism from some Grand Theft Auto fans, who have commented on the lack of realism.

"you can't commit 9/11 in gta 6…" wrote X user @eveisthebastard. "'realism' smh…".

"people will undoubtably say stuff like this doesnt really matter and i would usually agree but when literally all the hype for this game has been 'wow look at all the details there are ten trillion things being simulated' then yeah it really does matter," mentioned @fbq_2.

Meanwhile, others have argued that it's reasonable for developer Rockstar Games to prevent players from recreating the 9/11 attacks.

Industry observers note that "[The point of the game] is to commit crimes. Not be a terrorist," wrote @_MiisterJ. "Why would a game let you recreate 9/11?... Out of everything the game has to offer you draw the line at doing 9/11??".

Some have suggested that GTA 6's unusual interactions between planes and buildings may be the result of bugs. Launch day bugs are common in upcoming video games, with developers often issuing patches to fix them later on. Considering the strange behaviour of GTA 6's planes, particularly when compared to GTA 5, the idea that these are errors seems like a reasonable theory.

Recent findings suggest that however, other social media users have attributed the viral videos of pristine planes to a toggle in GTA 6's settings. Found under gameplay settings, GTA 6 includes a Reduced Vehicle Damage toggle which increases the amount of abuse your car or plane can take. Though it hasn't been confirmed that this setting was responsible for the nonsensical plane-building interactions seen in widely spread GTA 6 clips, activating it could theoretically help prevent vehicles from becoming deadly fireballs.

It has been revealed that further GTA 6 gameplay videos have supported suggestions that the viral clips are unusual by capturing more typically expected interactions between buildings and planes. A clip from Twitch streamer ohnePixel shows his small plane exploding after he flies it into a building, though like in GTA 5 the building itself remains undamaged. Another video shared on X by @muaxh03 shows a plane being destroyed after its left wing hits a building, killing the player character.

Industry observers note that in an interview with Love magazine, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson stated that GTA 6 attempts to balance realism with immersion, indicating that it may deviate where strict adherence to reality would make the game less fun. Whether this includes declining to realistically depict what happens when a jet flies into a highrise will likely become clearer as more people jump in to play.   • Industry observers note that buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive!
  • Trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive! Season 4 is upon us, and we're ready to be dragged back into the creepy woods of teen chaos and middle-aged mayhem. The Season 3 finale offered some major moments, including the revelation of the Pit Girl's identity and Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) sending out a distress call to the civilized world.

Trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home. However, if the first three seasons have taught us anything, it's that you can take the girl out of the wilderness, but you can't take the wilderness out of the girl. In both the past and present timelines, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse/Melanie Lynskey), Misty (Samantha Hanratty/Christina Ricci), and Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown/Tawny Cypress) are grappling for survival and control, so buckle up for a wild ride.

But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.

And keep an eye on this space — the final season of Yellowjackets is sure to see more folks fall, and we'll be updating this list accordingly.

Sources indicate that also, wherever possible, we have images with sliders of before and after. Slide 'em if you can stomach it.

Having just moved up from the junior varsity team, Rachel has the grim distinction of being the first Yellowjacket to die. Like the plane's pilots, she died in the crash, from a laceration to her throat.

In a recent development, father of Travis and Javi, Coach Bill (Carlos Sanz) died as a result of the plane crash that dropped the team in the Canadian wilderness. He'd fallen out of the plane into a tree. In an added bit of brutality, he died in front of Travis, as the teen boy tried to save him from his painful perch in a tree.

Good Christian girl Laura Lee (Jane Widdop) died a hero. After the team found an intact plane in the wilderness, Laura Lee began reading the manual to figure out how to fly it. She eventually took off with her teddy bear Leonard — and her personal lord and savior Jesus — as her co-pilots. But the plane exploded in the air, killing Laura and the Yellowjackets' chance of sending out a member for help.

The queen bee who couldn't hack it in the cabin, Jackie (Ella Purnell) froze to death while sleeping outside. And then she had the bizarre honor of becoming the first to be eaten by the team.

It has been revealed that travis's younger brother Javi (Luciano Leroux) would also be eaten, though the Yellowjackets weren't directly to blame for his death. While the team was hunting Natalie, Javi offered her a hiding place. But before they could get to safety, he fell through the ice of a frozen lake and died. From there, he was eaten.

In a recent development, despite the best efforts of the team, Shauna's baby was stillborn. This was a sad one.

Sources indicate that remember when Misty made a friend? She and Kristen (who was dubbed Crystal the Pistol by the team) bonded in the wilderness over their shared love of music and Steel Magnolias. They grew close enough that Misty shared her secret about destroying the plane's emergency transmitter, which Kristen — understandably — judged. From there, Misty pushed her off a cliff, and proclaimed the girl "missing.".

Real talk: Ben (Steven Krueger) lived way longer than we expected. The plane crash severely damaged his leg, which Misty then amputated on the spot. And incredibly, he survived possible infection, likely starvation, and the burning down of the cabin. But he couldn't escape the Yellowjackets. In a kangaroo court, they convicted him for the cabin's fiery annihilation (despite Misty's best efforts of a defense), and Taissa was chosen to carry out the execution. However, this was not how Ben died. Instead, he was tortured with crippling violence and deplorable conditions — that is, until Natalie took mercy on him and stabbed him fatally in the heart.

Recent findings suggest that poor Edwin (Nelson Franklin) just wanted to study frogs with his colleague Hannah (Ashley Sutton) and their guide Kodiak (Joel McHale). But then he stumbled in the Yellowjackets camp as they were feasting on Ben's remains. And, well, Lottie welcomed him with an axe to the head. RIP Edwin.

After Edwin was killed, the Yellowjackets imprisoned his surviving friends like they did Ben. When Kodiak tried to escape, he wasn't ended by the girls but by Hannah, who stabbed him in the eye. This was Hannah's bid to show the girls she could be trusted to keep their secret. And it got her through the rest of Season 3 at least.

According to recent reports, yellowjackets began — to quote Sarah McLachlan — building a mystery by introducing the show with the death of the Pit Girl. Underdressed for the snowy weather, she raced through the woods, pursued by masked figures, and ultimately fell into a pit of spikes, which killed her. Season 3 revealed her identity: Mari Ibarra (Alexa Barajas), a persistent rival of Shauna's. Mari too was eaten.

Recent findings suggest that how Travis (Andres Soto) died was a big mystery in Season 1, with a real bummer of a reveal. In the present, accidentally hanged himself while attempting to talk to the darkness. Lottie was supposed to save him but had a technical malfunction.

It has been revealed that in Season 1, Adam Martin (Peter Gadiot) was a mechanic who was having an affair with Shauna. But when Shauna began to suspect he had betrayed her, she stabbed him to death. His murder was covered up with the help of Misty, Nat, Taissa, and Jeff, because Yellowjackets are ride or die. (Sometimes both!).

Masquerading as a journalist, Jessica Roberts (Rekha Sharma) got on the wrong side of Misty Quigley, who fatally poisoned her with fentanyl-laced cigarettes.

Sources indicate that taisaa's family pet was murdered by Night Taissa. Then, his head was placed on creepy basement altar, which would prove a foreshadowing for Ben's fate.

Industry observers note that in Season 2, Detective Kevyn Tan (Alex Wyndham) was put in the awkward position of investigating his former high school classmates as he looked into the disappearance of Adam Martin. When his search led him to Lottie's cult's headquarters, he was felled — not by a Yellowjacket! — but by one of their fans. Specifically, Walter Tattersall (Elijah Wood), a citizen detective who fell for Misty. As the two were talking, Walter subtly poisoned Kevyn with a laced hot cocoa.

It has been revealed that nat (Juliette Lewis) died in the Season 2 finale, and we're still not over it. Of all the survivors, she seemed the one who likely to succeed in escaping their past. Worse yet, she was killed by her friend, Misty.

It has been revealed that it was an accident. Misty was trying to kill one of Lottie's cult members, Lisa (Nicole Maines), but Nat intervened by throwing her own body in front of the syringe, which was filled with poison. However, Natalie's story continued in the flashbacks. And yet, that only promised to make her ending sadder.

According to recent reports, who killed Lottie Matthews (Simone Kessell)? Well, to the surprise of many, it wasn't Shauna. It was her daughter, Callie Sadecki (Sarah Desjardins). Sure, Callie and Lottie had bonded, no matter how much that enraged Shauna. But when Callie confronted Lottie about stealing the incriminating DAT tape from the Sadecki home, Lottie began saying cryptic things about how Callie was a child of the Wilderness' darkness. In a rage, Callie reacted by shoving Lottie down the stairs.

Sources indicate that taissa's high school paramour (Liv Hewson) rejoined to the fold to reignite their romance and proved a solid teammate (Lauren Ambrose) in the present timeline. But their bliss was punctured by Van's cancer diagnosis, and yet that was not how she died! Hopeful the whatever of the wilderness would save her if she sacrificed someone else, Van tried to kill Melissa (Hilary Swank), a ball-capped Yellowjacket who was long thought dead, but had resurfaced under weird circumstances.

It has been revealed that ultimately, however, Van decided not kill Melissa. And in response, Melissa fatally stabbed her and fled, leaving Taissa to bury Van in an unmarked grave. Naturally, she took the opportunity to cut her lover open and eat her heart.

Industry observers note that don't be overwhelmed or waste an hour scrolling through your services to determine what to watch. We've got your back, whatever your mood. Mashable offers watch guides for all of the above, broken down by genre: comedy, thriller, horror, documentary, and animation, among others. But if you're seeking something brand newly introduced (or just new to streaming), we've got you covered there, too.

Sources indicate that darius Rucker rose to fame in the '90s as the frontman of the rock band Hootie & the Blowfish. In the 2000s, he went solo, first in R&B, then country music. Now, he looks back on a journey that included fame, fortune, struggles with drugs and alcohol, a marriage that fell apart, and much, much more.

Industry observers note that directed by Jason Bergh, Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie promises fans a look into the life and music that's kept its subject rolling for decades, with more to come. — Kristy Puchko, Entertainment Editor.

How to watch: Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie is now streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

Industry observers note that after seven seasons on Netflix, The Circle seemed like it had its last round. However, fans of the popularity-based competition reality show can catch the series in its new home on Hulu, with Season 8 landing this week on the streamer. This time around, the competitors will be both civilians and celebrities, who will vie for ultimate social dominance in the show's apartment block — whether playing as themselves or catfishing the others.

Sadly, the Hulu series will not have Netflix host Michelle Buteau, who hosted all seven seasons of the Netflix series. Instead, creator Tinx aka Christina Najjar will have immaculate shoes to fill as the upcoming Circle host. — Shannon Connellan, Senior Editor.

How to watch: The Circle is now streaming on Hulu.

Recent findings suggest that nicolas Cage is John Madden in a film you can either watch or not — it's your life. The Hollywood star leads American Hustle director David O. Russell's sports biopic, which follows Madden's NFL coaching and commentary career through to the development of EA Sports' Madden games. In particular, the film explores his partnership with Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis (Christian Bale) and the team's first ever Super Bowl victory in 1977. There's football history, ample prosthetics, and Cage-style roaring from the sidelines, so there might be something in here for you. — S.C.

Starring: Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney, and Shane Gillis.

How to watch: Madden is now streaming on Prime Video.

HBO's latest documentary paints a personal portrait of the people behind Never Use Alone, the confidential, anonymous, volunteer-operated hotline for people using drugs by themselves — people who don't have someone in their life they could (or feel they could) call for help in an emergency.

Written and directed by Ricki Stern and Jesse Sweet, the short documentary speaks to people who have used or volunteer for the U.S. National Overdose Response Spotting service, who alert emergency services to caller locations if they stop responding while using. Notably, the Trump administration has been moving from "harm reduction" approaches to drug use, including restricting federal funding to support overdose hotlines. The Hotline encapsulates why these grassroots programs are so vital. — S.C.

How to watch: The Hotline is now streaming on HBO.

Recent findings suggest that the collapse of crypto exchange FTX is one of the biggest stories of the tech world in recent years. Now, it comes to Netflix in The Altruists, inspired by New York Magazine articles by Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner.

Industry observers note that anthony Boyle plays FTX founder and former CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, while Emmy winner Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, CEO of FTX's sister organization Alameda Research. The Altruists examines their relationship, as well as their larger journey from idealists trying to change the global financial system to fraudsters accused of stealing billions.* — Belen Edwards, Entertainment Reporter.

Starring: Julia Garner, Anthony Boyle, Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Naomi Okada, Madison Hu, Matt Rife, and Eugene Young.

How to watch: The Altruists is now streaming on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that the global obsession with Formula 1 will not hit the brakes anytime soon, nor will the women driving to victory in the sport. In a new documentary from Disney+, you'll go behind the scenes of the F1 Academy, the all-female Formula 1 racing championship series launched in 2023. The film particularly focuses on the 2025 F1 Academy season, following drivers Maya Weug, Doriane Pin, Alisha Palmowski, and Chloe Chambers through the competition, and giving you a look at what it takes to get on the hallowed F1 track. — S.C.

Starring: Maya Weug, Chloe Chambers, Alisha Palmowski, and Doriane Pin.

How to watch: The Pursuit: F1 Academy is now streaming on Disney+.

Industry observers note that english comedian Oobah Butler has mastered the art of the prank. In 2017, he created fake restaurant The Shed at Dulwich, which became TripAdvisor's top-rated restaurant in London, all without serving a single meal. That same year, he "bullshitted" his way to the top of Paris fashion week by posing as a designer. Since then, he's created documentaries about infiltrating Amazon and getting funding for business ventures. This week, he releases a five-part HBO and A24 series, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

Throughout the series, Butler sets up scams aimed to target five different topics: wellness, wine, dating apps that use AI, music, and royalty. Based on the trailer, his ideas range from pitching a serum made of children's tears to communicating via remote control butt plug. If you love Nathan Fielder's Nathan for You business propositions but wish they were even more out there, this is the show for you. — B.E.

Sources indicate that how to watch: Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow premieres Nov. 22 at 11 p.m. ET on HBO and HBO Max.

Though Gentle Monster explores a dark, difficult subject, Léa Seydoux delivers a commanding performance as a woman facing shocking truths in her own family.

Written and directed by Corsage's Marie Kreutzer, the film centres on concert pianist Lucy (Seydoux) — and the film's music, by Camille, is an eclectic pop triumph. Captured with elegance and empathy by director of photography Judith Kaufmann, Lucy's idyllic life with her adoring husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) and young son is shattered when the police (led by an excellent Jella Haase as Detective Elsa Kühn) show up with a search warrant, accusing Phillip of a heinous crime. Forced to reckon with the accusations and view the person she loves through an unthinkable new lens, Lucy will never be the same — and it's within this nuance and emotional complexity that Seydoux thrives. — S.C.

Starring: Léa Seydoux, Jella Haase, Laurence Rupp, Malo Blanchet, Anton Rubtsov, Nils Strunk, Sylvester Groth, Patrycja Ziółkowska, Regina Fritsch, and Catherine Deneuve.

How to watch: Gentle Monster is now streaming on Netflix.

The wrongful conviction of Alfred Chestnut, Andrew Stewart, and Ransom Watkins (the so-called Harlem Park Three) is the focus of HBO's upcoming documentary, When a Witness Recants.

It has been revealed that directed by Dawn Porter and produced by Ta-Nehisi Coates, the film examines the miscarriage of justice that occurred in Baltimore, Maryland, when the three innocent 16-year-olds were sentenced to life in prison for the murder of 14-year-old DeWitt Duckett in 1983. Featuring interviews with Chestnut, Stewart, and Watkins, the film explores the 36 years they wrongfully spent in prison, the failures of the Baltimore Police Department, and their path to freedom and exoneration in 2019. — S.C.

How to watch: When a Witness Recants is now streaming on HBO Max.

American author Patricia Highsmith wrote a string of sensational thriller novels, but she's best known for created Tom Ripley, the killer con man who's spawned a series of adaptations all his own.

In A Talent For Murder, however, the Ripley adaptation gets a new, riveting wrinkle. Helen Mirren stars as Highsmith, who's living in a remote cabin in Switzerland when an ambitious young American man (Alden Ehrenreich) comes calling. He wants her to write another Ripley novel, to appease his publisher bosses back in the states. She wants a mind to mess with, and he's seductively willing. While he romances a beguiling young woman (Olivia Cooke), author and admirer join forces to imagine a fictional scenario worth of Ripley. What's fantasy and what's reality? The lines blur in this sexy and wickedly entertaining film. As I cheered in my review out of TIFF, "A Talent For Murder is darkly funny, freshly thrilling, and unrepentantly seductive. It's not a Ripley sequel, but it's damn close." — K.P.

Starring: Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, and Olivia Cooke.

How to watch: A Talent for Murder is now available for rent or purchase on Prime Video, Apple TV, and Fandango at Home.

Comedy nerds, you have to see this one.

The full title of this superb documentary from Nick Davis is You Had to Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (in a Canadian Kind of Way). Its focus is looking back at the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, which boasted such not-yet-famous performers as Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer. And most of the above offer interviews, home movies, and personal recordings of this pivotal moment in Canadian comedy.

Industry observers note that this movie was one of my absolute favorites at last year's Toronto International Film Festival. And as I cheered in my review, "You Had to Be There gifts audiences plenty of laughs, and so much more. This is not some fluffy celebration of comedians or even Godspell. Davis and company have come together to craft a documentary that is both informative, historical, entertaining, and deeply humane."* — K.P.

Starring: Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer.

How to watch: You Had to Be There is now available for purchase on Apple TV and Fandango at Home.

Directed by John Ripa and Alyce Tzue, Steps is a soft-goth twist on Cinderella. Centered not on on the famous princess (Amanda Seyfried) but her so-called evil stepsister Lilith (Ali Wong), this animated adventure offers a tale of rebellion, regret, sisterhood, and magic. The story you thought you know gets a fun shake-up that includes not only a fairy godmother (Bette Midler) and a charming prince (Daniel Radcliffe), but also a chipper talking frog (Stephanie Hsu), a medieval mean girl (Nikki Glaser), and a hot troll (Young Mazino).

Whether you've got a kiddo who's gotten a little too old for the standard Disney Princess fare, or you can't get enough of fractured fairytales, Steps is sure to please. As I wrote in my review, "Cheers to the small army of writers who've earned screenplay and story-by credits on this film (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, Felicia Ho, Riki Lindhome, and Kate Micucci). Steps gives audiences a familiar dose of fairy-tale tropes, then uses them to explore topics that can be tricky to explain to kids... But it's through the conflict of two sisters — one privileged and playing by the rules, the other marginalized and defiant — that each learns how to be better and more loving to themselves and each other. And kindness is contagious." — K.P.

Starring: Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Stephanie Hsu, Nikki Glaser, Daniel Radcliffe, Young Mazino, Peter Dinklage, and Bette Midler.

It has been revealed that how to watch: Steps debuts on Netflix on Nov. 20.

In its third season, Percy Jackson and the Olympians moves beyond the ground covered by the movies, giving Rick Riordan fans their first onscreen adaptation of The Titan's Curse. That means it's time to give a warm welcome to Bianca and Nico di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie and Levi Chrisopulos), two fan-favorite characters making their screen debuts this season.

Industry observers note that the arrival of Bianca and Nico isn't the only major change shaking up Camp Half-Blood this season. Thalia (Tamara Smart) is back, which means Percy (Walker Scobell) is no longer the only child of the Significant Three at camp. As these two embark on a quest to save a kidnapped Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) and the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen), will they get along? Or will they turn on one another in a conflict of mythic proportions? Book fans know that The Titan's Curse is where things get dark, so be warned. But don't worry: At least we know we'll be getting dam jokes.* — B.E.

According to recent reports, starring: Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries, Aryan Simhadri, Dior Goodjohn, Daniel Diemer, Charlie Bushnell, Tamara Smart, Olive Abercrombie, Levi Chrisopulos, Dafne Keen, Saara Chaudry, Ming-Na Wen, Hubert Smielecki, Jesse L. Martin, and Holt McCallany.

Recent findings suggest that how to watch: Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 premieres Nov. 20 on Disney+, with new episodes weekly.

Buzz, buzz! The Yellowjackets are back for their fourth and final season. In past and present timelines, the Yellowjackets are dropping like flies. We can't wait to see how things shake out for Shauna, Misty, Tai, and Melissa. (And Jeff!).

Last season ended with teen Natalie successfully escaping teen Shauna's hunt to use the frog scientist's repaired SAT phone to call for help. But anyone who can count can take a look at the Season 4 trailer and see that not all of residents of Camp Yellowjacket will make it back to civilization. This season we're likely to learn what happened to Hannah and Akilah. But will the show finally reveal the mysteries of the wilderness? What does that symbol mean? And of the still-standing Yellowjackets in the present-day timeline, who'll make it alive to season's end? — K.P.

Starring: Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, Tawny Cypress, Warren Kole, Sarah Desjardins, Hilary Swank, Sophie Nélisse, Sophie Thatcher, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Samantha Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, Liv Hewson, Kevin Alves, Jenna Burgess, and Nia Sondaya.

Sources indicate that how to watch: Yellowjackets Season 4 premieres Nov. 20 on Paramount+.

In a recent development, thanks to Don Bluth, we have magical and thrilling animated adventures like The Secret of NIMH, The Land Before Time, An American Tail, Anastasia, and All Dogs Go to Heaven. Now, documentarians Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker take a look back at this American animator's life and works, with the documentary Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There.

The film ushers audiences back to the early days of Bluth's life as a little boy inspired by Walt Disney's groundbreaking animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarves. Then, through archival footage, clips from a variety of animated films — including Bluth's — and interviews with the man himself, Somewhere Out There charts the dizzying highs and devastating lows that seemed to come with every project. There's a story about payments coming in a paper bag that's sure to have you cracking up. But most of all, it's riveting how candid Bluth is, whether recounting his animation firm's rivalry with the Disney studio or his own personal struggles.

A must-see for any true animation lover, Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is not to be missed. —K.P.

How to watch: Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is now available on VOD.

It has been revealed that like Odysseus (Matt Damon) landing on the shores of Ithaca after 20 years away, The Odyssey is finally coming home. Christopher Nolan's epic hits digital this week, complete with 90 minutes of bonus features. That means you can watch from your couch (just the way Nolan intended) as Odysseus braves the cyclops Polyphemus, Laestrygonian warriors, and a sniveling Robert Pattinson on his way back to his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) and his son Telemachus (Tom Holland). If you purchase the digital edition, you'll also get access to 90 minutes of bonus features.

Recent findings suggest that one of the best films of the year, The Odyssey pushes Nolan to stranger, more grotesque places than ever before, and the result is spectacular. Starring: Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Zendaya, and Charlize Theron.

#1437. Japan has a word for our dopamine-addicted internet brains: Dopagaki

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1621 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Japan has a word for our dopamine-addicted internet brains: Dopagaki

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forty-five minutes on TikTok can pass in the blink of an eye.
  • In Japan, there's a word for this particular kind of digital restlessness: dopagaki.
  • In a recent development, roughly translating to "dopamine brat," the Japanese slang term combines dopamine with "gaki," a disparaging word for a child, to describe someone who craves a steady stream of stimulation, whether it's short-form videos, social media, or fast-paced entertainment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forty-five minutes on TikTok can pass in the blink of an eye. Two minutes watching a video at normal speed? An eternity. Somewhere between scrolling through Instagram Reels, checking our phones during movies, and skipping to the best part of a song, our relationship with entertainment has become a little absurd. We're consuming more of it than ever, yet we seem to have less patience for any individual piece of it.

In Japan, there's a word for this particular kind of digital restlessness: dopagaki.

In a recent development, roughly translating to "dopamine brat," the Japanese slang term combines dopamine with "gaki," a disparaging word for a child, to describe someone who craves a steady stream of stimulation, whether it's short-form videos, social media, or fast-paced entertainment. But while dopagaki might sound like Japan's answer to the American "iPad kid," its reported origins are a little more surprising. The expression has been linked to a viral post about the structure of a pop song, and some of the young people it appears to mock have started using it to describe themselves.

So, a word associated with mocking a generation's appetite for instant gratification and excessive screen time has become a self-aware joke about the way we consume media. But dopagaki states just as much about the entertainment itself, packaged to deliver one satisfying moment after another, as it does about the people consuming it.

After all, when something new is always just a swipe away, is it any wonder we've grown impatient waiting for it?

Dopagaki (ドパガキ) is an abbreviation of the Japanese phrase "dōpamin chūdoku no gaki," or "dopamine-addicted brat." It describes someone who constantly craves quick bursts of stimulation, whether that's endlessly scrolling through TikTok, playing video games, or skipping ahead in longer videos to get to the good parts. Even platforms like YouTube have made this kind of consumption easier, with features like video chapters that let viewers jump straight to the moments they want to see.

It has been revealed that the word itself isn't particularly kind. In Japanese, "gaki" is a dismissive term for a child, closer to "brat" than "kid." And despite the reference to dopamine, dopagaki isn't a medical diagnosis. Dopamine plays a role in motivation, learning, and reward, and enjoying hyperstimulating entertainment doesn't necessarily mean someone is addicted to it.

Industry observers note that but the expression's reported origins reveal something interesting about the way we consume that entertainment. It wasn't a TikTok video or a smartphone habit that inspired the term — it was a pop song.

In a recent development, in December 2024, a Japanese user on X described the structure of "Lilac," a song by popular Japanese rock band Mrs. GREEN APPLE, using the phrase "dōpamin chūdoku no gaki." The observation centered on the song's rapid succession of musical payoffs, with catchy melodies and energetic transitions arriving in quick succession. There's barely a moment for the listener to settle into one musical idea before another comes along to capture their attention.

Sources indicate that the original post didn't use the shortened form dopagaki, and it's unclear exactly when that abbreviation first appeared. But the musical reference offers an intriguing window into the larger cultural phenomenon. The conversation wasn't simply about people demanding constant stimulation. It was also about entertainment seemingly designed to satisfy that demand.

And that idea extends well beyond a single pop song. Think about the videos that change shots every few seconds, the rise of microdramas, or the way creators are encouraged to hook viewers in the first three seconds of a video before they've had a chance to scroll away. Each newly introduced moment promises something more exciting than the last. Entertainment isn't just competing for our attention anymore. It's testing our patience.

By the summer of 2026, dopagaki had made its way into Japanese youth slang.

Recent findings suggest that in June, Joshikosei Lab, a Japanese marketing research group focused on teenage girls, included dopagaki among seven trending expressions identified through a survey of 60 high school girls. The group described the term as a humorous, self-deprecating way of acknowledging digital overconsumption, including the habit of watching TikTok while drying your hair or taking a bath.

It's a small survey, not a definitive measure of how widely the term is used. Still, it points to an interesting development: Some of the young people who might otherwise be the targets of the insult are now using it to laugh at themselves.

Sources indicate that that doesn't mean dopagaki has lost its derogatory edge. Calling someone else a dopamine-addicted brat can still sound condescending, particularly when it's used to dismiss their tastes or suggest that an entire generation has lost the ability to concentrate. But describing yourself as dopagaki is something different. It's a way of recognizing your own habits, perhaps with a little embarrassment, and finding humor in how familiar they've become.

Recent findings suggest that it's also a distinctly internet-native way of processing a shared anxiety. Rather than having a serious conversation about digital dependency every time someone finds themselves scrolling past midnight, there's now a word that captures the experience in five Japanese characters.

According to recent reports, and apparently, the joke resonates. In a separate October survey of 94 Japanese high school girls, 16 percent named dopagaki as their most-used slang expression of 2026, while another 17 percent mentioned they'd encountered the term on social media but didn't use it themselves. The findings suggest that the expression has gained some recognition among young people, even if not everyone identifies with it.

Perhaps that's part of what makes dopagaki such a revealing piece of internet slang. It captures both the humor and the discomfort of recognizing our own habits in a culture that rarely gives us a reason to put our phones down.

American internet culture has developed its own vocabulary for our increasingly complicated relationship with screens.

There's the "iPad kid," a typically unflattering description of children raised with tablets seemingly glued to their hands. As Know Your Meme documents, the term gained traction on TikTok through videos mocking children so absorbed in their screens that they appear oblivious to the world around them. Then there's "brainrot," a term that's become both a criticism of mindless online consumption and an affectionate description of the absurd content people can't stop watching.

Dopagaki exists somewhere between the two. Like "iPad kid," it can carry a generational judgment, implying that young people have become dependent on screens and instant gratification. Like "brainrot," it can also function as a self-aware joke, a way of admitting that your own relationship with the internet might be a little excessive.

According to recent reports, but there's an important distinction. The iPad kid is often someone else's child, usually invoked as an example of what's wrong with the next generation. Dopagaki, at least in its more playful usage, can be a label people willingly apply to themselves. And the habits it describes hardly belong to one generation.

Adults scroll through TikTok during commercial breaks, check notifications in the middle of conversations, and watch television with a second screen in their hands. The same people who complain about children needing constant entertainment may struggle to get through a quiet moment without reaching for their own phones.

According to DataReportal's Digital 2027 Global Overview Report, which draws on research conducted in 2026, online adults spend an average of 19 hours and 18 minutes per week using social media and online video platforms. That's more than two and a half hours a day on average spent watching, scrolling, and consuming content.

Of course, there's nothing inherently wrong with enjoying short videos, high-energy music, or entertainment that gets straight to the point. The more interesting question is how much of our appetite for constant stimulation comes from personal habit, and how much is shaped by the digital environments we've built around ourselves.

Sources indicate that social platforms are designed to keep us watching, listening, and scrolling. Creators work within those systems, learning to capture attention swiftly and hold onto it for as long as possible. Audiences, in turn, grow accustomed to an internet where the next entertaining thing is always a swipe away. Our habits shape the content we consume, and that content shapes our expectations of what entertainment should deliver.

Industry observers note that which brings us back to dopagaki. What was used in one early post to describe the structure of a pop song has become a way to capture a much broader experience of living online. There's something fitting about young people turning that criticism into a joke, particularly when the adults judging their screen habits are often just as attached to their own devices.

#1419. Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2157 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke.
  • Sources indicate that in my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered.
  • So, my hopes were high when it was announced Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke. Praise was fervent for the fantasy romance that stars Olivia Colman as a lonely Fisherwoman who weds a Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård). Admittedly, I was invested at "Olivia Colman." But buzz around the spirited sex scenes suggested Wicker 4DX would be a rollicking good time. So, naturally, as a journalist, it was my job to find out.

Sources indicate that in my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered. It was great fun, but also a cinematic experience that fostered a sense of community among romance fans who don't want to hide their horniness. Here was a safe space to giggle and swoon without fear of judgment. It reminded me of the gleeful days of slumber parties, and what a treasure they were.

So, my hopes were high when it was announced Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.

The Canadian phenomenon went from streaming to theaters, playing two episodes at a clip for fans to rewatch together. Then, it was confirmed that episodes 5 and 6 would be getting the 4DX treatment. As Mashable's newly minted 4DX-pert, I was obliged to go.

It has been revealed that so, how did Heated Rivalry 4DX compare the Wicker 4DX? Let's get into it.

I can hear you gasping. But think about it! This isn't the early days of the forbidden romance between hockey rivals Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie). What played in 4DX were the episodes "I'll Believe in Anything" and "The Cottage.".

Sources indicate that this means the screening began with the awkward morning after another fumbled hook-up between Shane and Rose Landry (Sophie Nélisse). This episode is the one where they break up, and from there, where flirtations and hand-holding suggest the intimacy between Shane and Ilya is blossoming into a love neither can admit to. That is, until Ilya does say "I love you," over the phone, in a far-away tunnel in Russia (and in Russian).

It has been revealed that episode 5 is full of beautiful dramatic moments, including Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) celebrating his championship win by bringing his lover Kip (Robbie G.K.) onto the ice, and coming out publicly. But there aren't many lusty moments. So, the 4DX seats would tease the audience by thrumming in sync with the show's soundtrack or vibrating anytime a text message arrived.

Sources indicate that episode 6 finally offers some fooling around in Shane's bedroom and then the oral sex scene, where Ilya goes down on Shane as he takes a call from Hayden (Callan Potter). Fans hooted and laughed as the seats attempted to match the rhythm of Ilya's motions. But it doesn't compare to the rocking of Wicker, which offered multiple sex scenes. The first of them is on the wedding night between the Fisherwoman and the Wicker Husband, and the motion added was so thoughtfully rendered in seat-rocking that the audience cheered upon its climax.

Heated Rivalry 4DX cannot compete here, or rather, it doesn't, by focusing on the final two episodes.

According to recent reports, well, for one thing, the violence hits harder. After the funeral for Ilya's father, he gets into a physical confrontation with his brother Alexei (Slavic Rogozine), who thrusts the hockey star into a wall. Ilya responds in kind, and the audience gasped as our bodies were collectively slammed in the comfort of our seats.

Sources indicate that likewise, the brief hockey scenes has a fresh sense of immersion. In slo-mo scenes, the seats slowly but smoothly rocked from side to side, mimicking the motion of the players' hips as they skated. And as "I'll Believe in Anything" is the episode where Shane "gets [his] bell rung," that hit is hard. But not so hard you'll get a concussion.

In a recent development, of course, 4DX is more than just shimmying seats. Some charming elements included fog emitting from the front of the theater while Shane grills (too many) burgers at the cottage. Or, when Ilya is playing in the hotel pool with children or splashing in the lake near the cottage, a spritz of water was emitted. The aim seemed to be off for me and my guest, as we could see the water rise and hiss of the propulsion, but we never actually got wet, or even misted. A mist opportunity, then?

And speaking of missed opportunities, I was actually disappointed that 4DX didn't use snow.

It's an element that I saw in Wicker 4DX and was quite awed by. And it might have been mindfully employed in the tunnel scene, as snow falls in the distance as Ilya pours his heart out over the phone. In this scene, 4DX did offer a slight breeze, which was a little chilly and did enhance the experience, making it feel more like we were out in the night with this lonely lover. But snow would have been a marvelous touch.

That's not something I thought I'd ever write. But here we are.

In Wicker, I was wowed by the smell of a wet forest and of fire catching. In Heated Rivalry, I could smell the chlorine of the pool in the aforementioned hotel scene and the scent of an ice rink in the arena sequences. I could hear the hiss of the machine that emits odor throughout the two episodes. But whether it was a beach scene, the burger grilling scene, or lakeside, I couldn't smell anything but a vaguely chemical smell.

I even thought perhaps own nose was the issue, perhaps stuffy from the radical weather changes that have been hitting New York City. My sniff test was putting my bottled ice tea under my nose, but I could make out the earthy smell of the tea and the hint of lemon, and even the whiff of my perfume as my wrist raised near my nose. So, not human error!

For the sake of science, I did attend the exact same 4DX theater as I did for Wicker, though this time my seats were in the last row instead of near the front. This shouldn't have impacted the smells or splashing though. And it did have one major drawback.

Online fans of this series have ranged from enthusiastic to feral. In person, it's similarly a mixed bag. Walking into the theater, I immediately clocked fans wearing Heated Rivalry merch, like T-shirts with Shane and/or Ilya on them, jerseys with the fictional hockey teams logos, and a ball cap embroidered with "I'm coming to the cottage.".

Like with Wicker DX, the energy was joyful and excited. People chatted and snacked. And I was surprised that the theater was not totally packed. But as the trailers started, more people came in. The seats slowly filled, some with fans loaded down with snacks. I will admit, my earlier 4DX experience informed our behavior here. My guest and I did buy snacks: chicken tenders, fries, and hot dogs with drinks. But we also got to the theater early enough to eat before the 4DX of it all kicked off. I'd remembered it being tricky to even eat popcorn in Wicker 4DX, in part because I'd not seen the movie before and so could not predict when my seat might buck.

Shout-out to the poor fellow to my left. He sat down during the trailers, unaware that some trailers have motion-activated moments in 4DX. As our seats bobbed up and down unexpectedly during a trailer for Disney's Hexed, I heard him gasp. I turned just in time to see the nachos leap up from their cardboard tray and into the open bag on his lap. "Oh, come on!" he yelped in righteous dismay. He was a gentleman, and tended to this snack-tastrophe as quietly as could be expected. So, this is less a scolding and more a warning: Choose your snacks and timing wisely in 4DX.

Sources indicate that the others around me were far less mindful of others. Two women to our right talked the whole time, as if they were watching at home. Yes, they even chattered while Shane maps out their whole could-be life together in bed at the cottage. Then there was the gaggle of women who collectively left together (presumably to re-snack or use the bathroom) and made a ruckus as they went, and then used flashlights when they got back to locate something misplaced in the shuffle. Lastly, there was the woman in front of me, who kept recording the screen with her phone.

Look, I'm no fan of using phones in a theater. For one, it's a place of immersion, where we are meant to shut out the outside world. For another, it's a place of community. However slick you think you're being, you absolutely are disturbing those around you when you pull out a device that is essentially a beam of light in a dark room.

But hey, I realize 4DX is a less serious cinematic experience. It's basically movie meets ride. And so I did expect to see some phones pop up for bits of the screening, as I'd seen plenty of POV videos from Wicker 4DX's run. However, this Heated Rivalry fan was recording her clips and then logging into Instagram to post immediately after. Plus, her brightness was SO high that I could tell you her name, or at least her Insta handle.

Recent findings suggest that behavior like this disrupts other people's immersion into what they paid to see. While the recorder might be looking to build online community (or cachet) through the clips, they're essentially ignoring those around them in favor of this aim. It's sacrificing not only the recorder's ability to live in the moment of the movie (or show) but also others, without their okay.

Sources indicate that still, despite these anti-social choices, there were moments of glorious fan unity in Heated Rivalry 4DX. When Wolf Parade's song "I'll Believe in Anything" began to play, there was a frisson in the air that had nothing to do with pipes, odors, or shaking seats. The theater was silent as we all watched and pined for the happy ending we know by heart by now. As Kip took to the ice, I could hear choked gasps of anticipation. When Scott kisses him, there were cheers and applause. Then, when Ilya notes the line ("I'm coming to the cottage"), the audience roared with excitement as if we'd won the Stanley Cup. Plus, they were chirps and cheers throughout the final sequence of episode 6, where Shane comes out to his parents and Ilya uses the word "boyfriend" for the first time.

Industry observers note that in those moments, it was a pleasure to be in that crowd. And yet, it was easier to enjoy Wicker.

Industry observers note that I can't be certain, but I could guess based on release dates that fewer people in the Wicker 4DX had seen the production before their showtime than was true of Heated Rivalry. The most ardent loons I know have seen the Crave series top to bottom five or six times. And perhaps that means that rather than coming for a whole experience, these 4DX attendees were coming for massive emotional moments. Those don't really translate into big physical motions.

While this is a streaming drama series that does a lot of things beautifully, it's stretches of earnest dialogue don't make for the kind of unserious fun the romantic comedy of Wicker allowed for. Still, it was a fun night out to relish in a show I love with friends and fellow fans.

According to recent reports, my advice to you, should more showtimes be added, would be if you go to Heated Rivalry 4DX, zip your lip and put your phone away. And look, if you do plan to pull out your phone, at least have enough consideration for your fellow audience member to do it with the brightness down, and maybe not smack dab in the middle of the theater. Don't make your short attention span or craving for content cachet someone else's problem.

#1415. Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.
  • In a recent development, the two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years.
  • In a recent development, scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.

In a recent development, the two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years. Then the giant swallowed the smaller star. The trapped star took only about seven years to spiral to the center, where the two merged into a single star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope supplied the final evidence.

In a recent development, scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely. In this case, the small star didn't survive. But in other pairs, the giant's gas gets blasted away first, leaving both stars in an orbit that takes just hours or days instead of years. Those tight pairs can later become black holes or super-dense dead star cores called neutron stars, or explode as supernovas. Some also send out gravitational waves, which are ripples in space and time.

Lead author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University, and an international team reported the discovery Wednesday in the journal Nature.

Industry observers note that the researchers nicknamed the larger star "Massive Bao," and it earned the name. It had about seven times the sun's mass and 350 times its width, shining 18,000 times brighter.

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said Karel Temmink, a doctoral student at Radboud University in the Netherlands, in a statement.

Its partner, "Little Bao," had about 70 percent of the sun's mass.

It has been revealed that stars like Big Bao swell up near the end of their lives. If our sun did the same, it could grow past Earth's orbit. As Big Bao swelled, Little Bao began skimming its outer layer and stripping away gas. Soon the small star was orbiting inside the giant. The gas there was spread so thin that Little Bao stayed intact for years, according to the paper. Still, the gas slowed it down, much like air slows a thrown ball, until it eventually sank toward the giant's core.

According to recent reports, no telescope can literally see inside a star. But friction from the small star's plunge churned the giant's gas and carried that heat to the surface. There it highlighted up as seven years of steady brightening. When the team compared the starlight from before and after the eruption — and tested computer models against it — the best explanation was a small star spiraling inside the giant.

Sources indicate that when the smaller one finally reached the giant core, gravity likely ripped it apart. That triggered a blast that hurled about one-tenth of the giant's outer material into space.

Their encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," mentioned Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia.

The explosion itself came on surprisingly fast. The team thought an outburst would take years. Instead, it took just a week from when its brightness started rising to its peak, said Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain.

Scientists expect many star pairs to go through this phase, but catching one in the act has taken incredible luck.

"The timescales involved are short, months to years, and the rates at which they form are low," astrophysicist Jason Nordhaus wrote in a commentary published alongside the study. "Just a few stars exist in this phase at any given time in a galaxy such as the Milky Way.".

Recent findings suggest that astronomers usually piece together star mergers long after they happen. This time, a fleet of telescopes followed Bao as the events unfolded. The team first noticed the star acting strangely in Feb. 2023, in data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. In Sep. 2024, another telescope saw it brightening and puffing out dust. In July 2025, NASA's Spherex telescope happened to catch it fading in visible light while it brightened in infrared light. Then, on Oct. 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky-scanning telescope in California, spotted the eruption.

Webb took its look on Dec. 24, 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. No telescope had ever followed up on an event like this so quickly, Karambelkar stated.

According to recent reports, what the newly single star, now just called "Bao," will become remains an open question. Only future observations will show how it settles down.

NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile will scan huge areas of sky over and over. They should spot events like this in hundreds of nearby galaxies.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar stated.

Check out our full review of the Sony XM4C headphones.

Anyone looking for the best blend of sound, comfort, and price: Sony brought back its viral XM4 headphones with the second-generation XM4Cs. The design remains unchanged from the first generation, but sound gets a boost, making them the best-sounding headphones under $300 I've tried, and a no-brainer for students, office workers, or anyone looking to get as close as possible to the flagship headphone experience, minus the price.

It has been revealed that plenty of $450 headphones don't feature 10-band equalizers. Sony's WH-1000XM4C headphones do. That mentioned, even if you don't like to mess around with a companion app, these headphones sound balanced and rich out of the box, making everything from classical piano concertos to classic rock shine. While their sound quality is certainly a huge draw, it's far from the only standout feature of these headphones.

Sources indicate that sony struck simplistic gold with the design of the XM4 headphones in 2020 — which is why some fans were sad to see the iconic look go in the XM5 and XM6 headphones. Now, prospective buyers don't have to decide between the latest tech and the coveted XM4 design. While Sony didn't add any improvements to the ANC (it still features the same four mics and QN1 processor it did in 2020), the internals of the sound quality make these a much easier (and easier to get) recommendation in 2026. Like the OG XM4s, these headphones also are relatively low profile, with plenty of cushioning in the headband and ear cups, minus any overbearing squeeze. The result is solid passive noise cancellation, with comfort enough to get you through a work or school day's worth of wear.

According to recent reports, the biggest cons of these headphones are that they lack spatial audio and the battery life got bumped down three hours from the first to the second gen — 30 to 27 hours. However, the 27-hour range still sits above other (more expensive) mid-range options, so it's not the most devastating loss. And at full price, they're still less than half the price of Sony's other 2026 release: the ultra-premium 1000X the Collexion headphones.

Check out our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

Sources indicate that people who like their headphones to make a statement: The Nothing Headphone (a) are going to turn some heads. The rectangular ear cup and semi-transparent design meld together the past and the future in a way that is unmistakably Nothing. Don't get me wrong, though; they don't just look good. These headphones pack a relatively balanced soundscape and decent ANC.

They're also the perfect headphones for anyone who isn't too great about plugging their devices in regularly, as they pack a whopping 75 hours of listening time per charge, with the ANC on.

Sources indicate that these are the best headphones Nothing makes, thanks to their combo of performance and value, and the value prop here is strong. When brainstorming the best headphones under $300, the Headphone (a) immediately came to mind because they offer something most budget-oriented headphones don't (or can't, due to budget constraints): an unmistakable style. These headphones aren't trying to dupe any other one on the market.

The power of the design doesn't stop there. The on-ear controls of these headphones are so intuitive, both in their function and placement, that I rarely reached for my device when wearing them.

In a recent development, as nice as the XM4C headphones are, they're still an investment. These Soundcore headphones keep performance high on the core features of headphones, while showing their price point in places that don't detract too much from the overall user experience.

Sources indicate that let's start with how they wear.
