Roblox money is pushing a controversial anorexia treatment

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 42 min read (8433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~42 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What studying the ketogenic diet for eating disorder patients tells us about the future of mental health research in the US.﻿.
  • Sources indicate that in a dark room, a man with a camera makes his pitch: Therapy isn’t the first treatment you should get if you have anorexia or bulimia, he states.
  • “Suddenly, that eating disorder is not there anymore,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What studying the ketogenic diet for eating disorder patients tells us about the future of mental health research in the US.﻿.

Sources indicate that in a dark room, a man with a camera makes his pitch: Therapy isn’t the first treatment you should get if you have anorexia or bulimia, he states. He’s in his late 20s, wearing a backward camo baseball cap and a silver chain. “Instead of going straight to the therapy, let’s do a keto diet where we encourage you to eat as much as you want” — all while limiting your carbohydrate intake to 30 grams a day. He tells his viewers that this shift will force your brain to use a different fuel source, and “all those defective neural pathways that were causing you to engage in that eating disorder, they heal up and they start to work correctly.”.

“Suddenly, that eating disorder is not there anymore,” he says.

Sources indicate that there is no evidence to support the man’s claim. In fact, most of the psychiatrists and nutritionists The Verge spoke with for this story said that treating an eating disorder with a restrictive diet is just too risky.

Recent findings suggest that “This intervention right now would be reasonably viewed as dangerous or high risk,” notes Kylie Jeffrey, a nutrition scientist at Duke University. “I think that’s a danger,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist and the founding director of the University of North Carolina’s Center of Excellence for Eating Disorders. “Don’t try this at home.”.

National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline: Call 1-866-662-1235 for help finding treatment options at all levels of care, or check the alliance’s national database for treatment options.

ANAD helpline: Call 1-888-375-7767 for emotional support and treatment referrals.

Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis.

988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well.

Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them.

As with many spurious health claims, this one didn’t come out of nowhere. The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, very low-carb diet that can cause people to go into “ketosis,” a state in which a person’s cells begin to burn fat, in the form of ketone bodies, instead of sugar. And researchers have started to study its use to treat anorexia nervosa. But because the research has barely begun, no one knows if this will work. And although some researchers think that trying to treat a disease involving food restriction with a limited diet might be dangerous, others are excited about the possibility of new treatments. They just want to see data from large, rigorous clinical trials to make sure that keto actually is a treatment.

According to recent reports, on the internet, however, the ketogenic diet is already being promoted as an “effective” way to treat eating disorders. The man in the camo hat — his name is Matthew — is an key part of how that message has spread. Matthew’s audience is small. He has a few thousand followers on YouTube and Instagram. And the video in which he talks about eating disorders going away on keto has a little under 1,000 views on YouTube at the time of reporting. But it would be a mistake to evaluate his reach and influence solely based on his view counts. Because in the “Make America Healthy Again”-coded world of ketogenic diet influencers, Matthew is about as connected as it gets.

It has been revealed that matthew’s father is David Baszucki, the CEO and cofounder of the gaming platform Roblox. It’s the largest gaming platform in the world, with more than 100 million daily active consumers, most of them kids and teens (though there are plenty of adults, too). Thanks to Roblox, his net worth sits somewhere between $3 billion and $5 billion. And since 2021, David and his wife Jan Ellison Baszucki have put more than $105 million toward funding research, clinical care, and advocacy work that revolves around metabolic health, with more than $55 million dedicated to the use of a ketogenic diet to treat mental illness. They’re considered significant players in this burgeoning space.

I first heard about the Baszuckis’ philanthropic interests in December 2025, when a podcast producer emailed me to ask if I would be interested in hosting a latest show funded by a nonprofit organization. Over the phone, I learned that the podcast would mainly be covering a new study by a researcher named Guido Frank in which scientists had investigated the use of the ketogenic diet to treat anorexia nervosa. I also learned that the nonprofit that had funded the study, Baszucki Group, would also be funding the podcast. I declined to participate in the project.

According to recent reports, the Baszuckis feel strongly about the impact of their philanthropy. “Baszucki Group has been the catalyst for a growing body of research targeting metabolic root causes of mental illness with therapeutic ketogenic interventions,” Baszucki Group spokesperson Maura Siefring wrote in an email to The Verge.

Matthew’s own compelling story is what got his parents interested in this kind of philanthropy — though that story has never included an eating disorder. “I healed my own bipolar disorder using a ketogenic diet,” Matthew notes in many of his videos. “And now I’m on a mission to help other people recover.” Keto is a specific area of interest for Matthew, who highlighted his parents’ role in funding this research in a June video called “This Keto Anorexia Study Just Broke the Internet.”.

“Broke the internet” is something of an overstatement. Still, Dr. Guido Frank, a psychiatrist at the University of California, San Diego, and the lead author of the trial, published in Communications Medicine, tells The Verge, “I am extremely hopeful that this could be — this is a little bit dramatic, but a game-changing intervention … I haven’t seen such good results throughout my whole career.”.

It has been revealed that in the small, 14-week study, which Frank’s team conducted with a $235,000 donation from the Baszuckis, researchers recruited 22 people who were either slightly underweight or weight “normalized,” meaning that they were neither overweight nor underweight. The goal was to see if it was safe and feasible to use the ketogenic diet as an anorexia treatment. Of the 18 people who completed the study, “none of them lost weight,” Frank indicates. But what’s remarkable, he says, is that 12 of those 18 participants experienced a decrease in their eating disorder and depression symptoms, such that they no longer met the diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa. “This is not something that you typically see in the other available treatments that we have.”.

Sources indicate that the study didn’t require that participants receive any form of therapy during the trial period, and if you asked Matthew, he might tell you that’s a good thing. His videos frequently proclaim the dangers of conventional psychiatric treatments. “There’s a malicious force trying to cripple us, trying to feed us this snake oil,” he indicates in a video posted in March. That seems to be a common refrain among ketogenic diet influencers.

Sources indicate that “There are a lot of people who are going to use metabolic psychiatry and the ketogenic diet to disparage psychiatry in a way that’s wholly inappropriate,” notes Dr. Drew Ramsey, a nutritional psychiatrist. “And that’s not helpful to patients and families because there are lots of people out there at the moment in full remission from their mental illness with the treatments that we have,” including therapy and medications — “millions and millions of people.”.

Sources indicate that for every dollar the government spent on research in the US, private funding sources — namely private industry — spent more than four, according to a 2022 estimate from the National Science Foundation. But that statistic hides an important fact about the kind of research that the federal government funds. The US government is the single largest source of funding for basic research — the kind of research that leads to health breakthroughs later on. It’s also the second-largest source of funding for health research, after industry. This is why it’s such a big problem that federal scientific funding has, on average, been on the decline in the US since 2000 — a problem that’s gotten worse under the Trump administration.

Recent findings suggest that in April, President Donald Trump fired the National Science Board, which caused the board’s grantmaking to slow to a near halt. NIH funding went down by 22 percent in 2025, compared with the average over the previous decade. As a result, the gap between federal funding and private funding has widened. In addition to industry, philanthropic funders have long played a role in helping US scientists carry out their work. Think Howard Hughes or Bill Gates. But now that federal research dollars are so hard to come by, the importance of private philanthropic funding has risen substantially.

Sources indicate that that makes billionaires like the Baszuckis very influential. By choosing to fund one type of research or one specific type of treatment, wealthy funders can play a significant role in setting the country’s scientific agenda for years to come. For example, researchers who are hoping to get funded might choose to write grant proposals that will please the Baszuckis, leaving other potential treatments for anorexia languishing — if only because it is too hard to find money to test them.

In a recent development, eating disorder research may be particularly vulnerable to this problem. About 30 million people in the United States will develop an eating disorder in their lifetime, but eating disorder research has long been underfunded. And the NIH’s annual anorexia funding was only $14 million in 2025, $4 million less than just two years before. Under the second Trump administration, millions in federal eating disorder research grants have been terminated.

Sources indicate that but talk to anorexia researchers, and they will tell you: Anorexia stands apart. Mainly, it is deadly, with one 2014 study finding that it has among the highest mortality risks of the major mental health conditions, behind only certain substance use disorders. And no medication has ever been approved in the US to treat it. Even commonly prescribed psychiatric drugs like SSRIs often aren’t effective against anorexia symptoms in underweight patients.

Because of this, psychotherapy continues to be the standard treatment for anorexia nervosa. But therapy, the good kind, is expensive and can be hard to access. This is a problem because the longer it takes to access treatment, the harder anorexia becomes to treat. And the reality is that half — “maybe more than half” — of anorexia patients don’t actually go into remission, says Dr. Amanda Downey, a psychiatrist at the University of California, San Francisco, who specializes in the treatment of adolescents and children with eating disorders.

Sources indicate that researchers in the field are hoping that a upcoming treatment will emerge. “We’re doing our best with what we have, but it’s just not good enough,” says Dr. Jennifer Derenne, a child and adolescent psychiatrist at Stanford University who specializes in anorexia.

“We’re doing our best with what we have, but it’s just not good enough.”.

By putting approximately $2 million toward anorexia research since 2023, the Baszuckis have paid for at least one ketogenic diet case series, one mouse study, and two small clinical trials, including one that’s still ongoing. That funding represents just over 4 percent of the total amount of NIH funding dedicated to anorexia research between 2023 and 2025 — not an earth-shattering amount. But it’s been enough to support something rare in anorexia research: the development of a novel treatment candidate.

It has been revealed that this dynamic is playing out across research medicine. As federal research dollars go down, private funders gain influence and power, to the point of steering entire fields toward certain research targets. And although some private funding institutions employ experts to help them decide where the money should go, others rely on the interests and intuitions of their billionaire founders.

That’s why it’s worth paying attention to the moves the Baszucki family has made over the past five years as they focus their attention on promoting a ketogenic diet as a treatment for a wide range of mental health conditions, including anorexia nervosa. They fund research they believe will support their conviction that this specific diet will change mental healthcare forever.

Caroline Beckwith is a 36-year-old artist and gym manager based in Brooklyn. She talks fast, in short, joyous bursts of words. Her family states her life was changed by a summer camp she attended at age 14. “She just had an inner light, and it went out, and it just was darkness,” says Dr. Barbara Scolnick, an internal medicine doctor based in Boston and Beckwith’s aunt.

In a recent development, beckwith started dieting along with some other girls in her bunk — and that soon morphed into an eating disorder. She hid it for a while; her parents both worked and they didn’t all eat dinner together, she tells me, and she’d lie about having eaten. But “then I lost a lot of weight,” she indicates.

Sources indicate that though Beckwith started seeing a therapist, her condition continued to get worse. Then, one day, Beckwith had a seizure while on a family outing in Manhattan. When the ambulance arrived, the EMT asked if Beckwith had any preexisting conditions, and Beckwith’s father reflexively mentioned no. That’s when Beckwith’s mother, Judith Scolnick, lost it.

“I screamed at the top of my lungs and noted, ‘She is anorexic and nobody’s doing anything about it!’” Scolnick states.

From that moment on, Beckwith’s parents did everything they could to get her the best possible care. She saw a psychiatrist at Mount Sinai’s eating disorder center. Then, at the age of 17, she was admitted to an inpatient eating disorder program at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore.

Industry observers note that her stay there helped her gain weight, but that was all. “When I was leaving, I was thinking, ‘Do these people think I’m better? Like, that’s crazy, because I’m definitely not.’” When it was time to apply to college, Beckwith remembers thinking, “‘I can’t make a strategy for the future at all. All I can think about is counting calories.’”.

Industry observers note that as a physician, Barbara Scolnick didn’t want to accept that anorexia would haunt her niece for the rest of her life. Speakers at medical conferences Scolnick attended in the late 2000s and early 2010s would often tell healthcare providers in the audience to examine a patient’s family, especially the mother, who might be controlling or cold. This is similar to the now discredited theory of “refrigerator mothers,” in which children with autism were once thought to have emotionally cold mothers. But Scolnick didn’t think her sister was like that. So hearing all these researchers repeatedly put the blame on patients’ families was infuriating, she notes. “It was just so stupid.”.

According to recent reports, so Scolnick did her own research. She spent hours in the medical school library at Harvard, reading old studies. And one day, she started reading about a doctor in the 1920s who developed a ketogenic diet as a way to reduce the incidence of seizures in children with diabetes. Around the same time, the ketogenic diet started being used as a treatment for epilepsy.

In a recent development, this was the first time she’d read about anyone doing better, medically, on a ketogenic diet, and it jogged her memory. Beckwith had told her stories about the early days of her disorder — that going on a diet and eating less felt incredible at first. “‘I felt so strong. I felt so… almost supernatural and powerful,’” Scolnick recalls Beckwith telling her. So Scolnick wondered: What if it was the ketones that had made Caroline feel good? Ketones are the fat-derived fuel the body uses as energy when sugar isn’t readily available. If ketones had made Caroline feel good when she’d started restricting, then maybe getting Beckwith to fuel her body with ketones, without restricting her calories, could help her body and her brain learn a new way to be.

It has been revealed that beckwith was 29 when she tried her aunt’s idea. She’s open about the fact that part of the appeal of going on a ketogenic diet was that people often use it to lose weight. But Beckwith, who wasn’t underweight at the time, didn’t lose weight on the ketogenic diet. Instead, she claims, she started to feel happier within a few days. One month in, “I felt like the majority of the thoughts were either — not, like, gone, but way less,” she says. The anorexia was still there, but it didn’t have the hold on her that it had had before she started on keto.

But not everything got better. Some things actually got worse. Beckwith started measuring parts of her body again — a form of “body checking,” which she hadn’t done in a long time. She started again because she was worried about putting on weight on this new high-fat diet. So although the thoughts she’d had for the past 15 years had gone mostly quiet, Beckwith still felt fragile, like she might tip back into restriction at any moment. “I feel like if I get the flu and lose two pounds or something, I will be anorexic again,” she told her aunt. “It’s so right there.”.

That’s when Scolnick suggested a second intervention that she’d read about: ketamine, a dissociative anesthetic that’s been used to treat PTSD and treatment-resistant depression. Beckwith completed four rounds of IV ketamine treatments at a clinic, but she notes the anorexia was completely gone after three.

Industry observers note that the day of her third round of ketamine, she went home and told the guy she’d been living with to move out. He hadn’t been paying rent, and she’d been trying to break up with him for a long time, but this was the first time she could speak to him clearly.

Then, “I called my parents and was like, ‘I don’t think I’m anorexic anymore.’” For 15 years, all Beckwith could think about was calories, and now those thoughts were gone. And without the constant distraction, she was able to be present in conversations with her family and with her friends. “Everything just got better and better every single day,” she says.

Sources indicate that but her recovery didn’t go down without side effects. Beckwith also experienced what she describes as a manic episode after that third dose of ketamine. For days she barely slept, staying up to make art and write instead.

Sources indicate that that worried Scolnick, who contacted Dr. Christopher Palmer, a Harvard psychiatrist, to ask for his advice. Scolnick and Beckwith say Palmer spoke with Beckwith and told her to take Tylenol PM for a few nights to help her sleep. She did, “and then everything settled,” she states. Beckwith opted for a fourth and final round of ketamine. (Palmer declined to comment on Beckwith’s care.).

According to recent reports, beckwith stayed on a ketogenic diet for around two years. Today, she prioritizes eating what she calls “healthy fats” and says she probably eats fewer carbs than the average American. But she eats pizza whenever she wants, and if there are bagels or donuts available at work, she doesn’t think twice about taking part. The fact that she isn’t tracking her carbohydrate intake hasn’t affected her recovery.

Beckwith’s anorexia never returned.

According to recent reports, scolnick’s idea about the ketogenic diet dovetails with a growing interest in the field of “metabolic psychiatry,” a term coined by Stanford University psychiatrist Dr. Shebani Sethi. The basic idea is that treating metabolic disorders, such as inflammation and high blood sugar, will also treat mental health conditions.

Industry observers note that there are reasons to believe this approach may be useful — people with high levels of inflammation appear to be less likely to respond well to psychiatric drugs. And some schizophrenia patients went into full remission when treated with anti-inflammatory drugs. Researchers have also found that certain autoimmune disorders that cause inflammation in the brain can also trigger psychosis.

In a recent development, ketogenic diets also have a long history in medicine, including the cases Scolnick read about. They’ve been explored as treatments for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, “with some mixed results,” states Stanford’s Derenne.

Industry observers note that in 2024, Sethi and a research team conducted a pilot trial of the ketogenic diet in people with bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, which was partly funded by the Baszuckis. The researchers found that participants lost weight, slept better, and were more satisfied with their lives. Participants’ psychiatric symptoms also improved.

Industry observers note that ramsey, the nutritional psychiatrist, claims the work is promising — but it’s just a pilot study. Those don’t determine if a treatment works, only that a larger trial can be done using a similar study design because the patients in it were able to follow the diet guidelines.

Recent findings suggest that to determine a treatment’s effectiveness, researchers typically look for large, randomized controlled trials. And although the research is heading in that direction, such a trial has yet to take place.

But what does human metabolism have to do with anorexia nervosa? Researchers have found unexpected links. Through a privately funded initiative, researchers highlighted in the 2010s that the risk of developing anorexia is influenced by eight areas of the human genome, some of which play crucial roles in metabolism. More recently, scientists found that a set of genes that increase the risk of developing anorexia nervosa are also associated with less risk for obesity and type 2 diabetes. These findings suggest that metabolism is involved in anorexia, indicates the University of North Carolina’s Bulik, who was part of the research team in both instances.

Sources indicate that if the idea of treating a mental health disorder with a ketogenic diet rings a bell, these findings likely aren’t the reason. In February, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made an unfounded claim that a ketogenic diet can “cure” schizophrenia, and the news spread from there.

In a recent development, kennedy was probably referencing the work of Christopher Palmer, the Harvard professor who helped with Beckwith’s post-ketamine side effects. Along with Sethi, Palmer is widely considered one of the foremost experts in the field of metabolic psychiatry. He’s published a number of case studies in which he describes how the symptoms of patients with various conditions, including mental health conditions, improved while on a ketogenic diet, sometimes to the point of “remission.” (In a recent paper, he also described cases in which certain patients experienced short episodes of mania after they started on keto.).

But the Harvard psychiatrist doesn’t claim the diet “cures” anything.

“It’s unfortunate that he used the word ‘cure,’” Palmer told The Harvard Crimson after RFK Jr.’s comment made headlines. “‘Cure’ implies that you can do the treatment for a short time, stop the treatment, and your illness never comes back,” he noted. “That’s not at all what I’ve seen in patients with severe mental illness.”.

Industry observers note that the MAHA embrace of “keto for mental health” seems to be part of a larger trend: In a country where millions don’t have access to healthcare and the public’s trust in science has noticeably declined, people will often adopt upcoming treatments if they’re marketed well enough. Take the boom in gray-market peptides, which gained popularity in large part because people didn’t have to go to a doctor to get them. From there, it was easy for the MAHA crowd to embrace them. Because MAHA isn’t just about embracing alternative treatments. The ethos also thrives on rejecting conventional ones.

According to recent reports, that makes metabolic psychiatry perfect for MAHA. It’s an emerging field that challenges conventional wisdom in psychiatry — long a target of the movement’s ire. Kennedy has publicly presented an “action proposal” to wean Americans off psychiatric medications, which he has falsely claimed cause mass shootings.

Recent findings suggest that I asked a Baszucki Group spokesperson if the billionaire couple identifies with the MAHA movement. I didn’t receive an answer. But the Baszuckis have left some hints. In September 2025, they donated $50 million to launch an organization called the Coalition for Metabolic Health, which claims that chronic disease “is largely preventable through dietary and lifestyle change that improves metabolism.” (Chronic diseases are often the result of a combination of factors that can also be heavily influenced by a person’s genetics, as well as by environmental factors that aren’t lifestyle-based.) And then there’s David Baszucki’s $5 million donation to the president’s ballroom fund. However, David Baszucki isn’t the one leading the charge in funding ketogenic diet research.

According to recent reports, that’s Jan Ellison Baszucki, Matthew’s mother, a former marketing executive and a novelist. She’s taken it upon herself to fund “all this research” and spread the word about the diet, Matthew stated during a talk he gave at the Metabolic Health Summit in 2024. As president of Baszucki Group, the nonprofit that Jan and David started to advance the family’s “philanthropic goals,” she plays a central role in funding ketogenic diet research. Jan is also the founder of a nonprofit called Metabolic Mind, which aims to make the ketogenic diet a mainstream treatment for mental health conditions. And of course, Matthew himself is skeptical about psychiatric care. On his own social media accounts, Matthew regularly bashes therapy and psychiatrists’ use of medications to treat patients, calling the latter “poisons with positive side effects.” That may be because of his own experience.

Sources indicate that in his second semester of college, Matthew was involuntarily hospitalized for 10 days at Stanford’s psychiatric hospital. That’s where he got a diagnosis of bipolar 1 with psychotic features. He was put on medications, which helped him, Jan remarked at an event sponsored by Metabolic Mind in 2022. But Matthew had a hard time taking his medications during manic periods, and the episodes kept happening. Sometimes he’d disappear, and Jan wondered if he would ever come home.

Then, in 2020, Jan spoke with Harvard’s Palmer, who suggested putting Matthew in ketosis. So, in January 2021, Matthew went on keto. “I think we knew within 10 or 12 weeks … that something miraculous was happening to my brain,” Matthew said on Keto Bipolar, a podcast he cohosts.

In a recent development, matthew’s turnaround was life-changing. And the Baszuckis wanted to get the word out about what happened. So they started funding ketogenic diet research via their newly formed foundation. They also debuted Metabolic Mind, which regularly posts testimonials from people who say they healed their mental illness using a ketogenic diet, as well as news about recently published studies, especially those they’ve funded. In 2024, Jan and Matthew appeared on the Today show together to promote keto as a mental health cure. Jan also executive produced a documentary called The Cholesterol Code, in which Matthew appeared, which challenges a well-established link between very high levels of LDL cholesterol and an increase in people’s risk of developing heart disease, even when those people are lean and considered otherwise metabolically healthy. The documentary, which promotes a ketogenic diet, centers around a study that has been critiqued and was retracted, at the request of its authors, in early March 2026, before the documentary’s theatrical premiere and digital release. The doc, which stars one of the study’s authors, was released in April anyway. And the paper was republished, with some changes, after that.

Matthew has given interviews and talks at events sponsored by Metabolic Mind. When speaking about anorexia and the ketogenic diet, Matthew makes statements that go far beyond what the science currently suggests. “We’ve never had a biological treatment that is this effective or that demonstrates such tremendous promise for anorexia nervosa as a ketogenic diet,” Matthew said in a recent video published on his YouTube account. Notably, Matthew’s YouTube account is featured on the Metabolic Mind website.

Industry observers note that anorexia doesn’t appear to have been on the Baszuckis’ radar as a funding target when they started handing out grants for ketogenic diet research in 2021. That may have changed after Jan was introduced to Barbara Scolnick and her twin sister by one of Barbara’s colleagues.

Beckwith’s keto and ketamine protocol helped her so much that Scolnick wanted the world to know about it. So, with her niece’s blessing, she published a detailed account of the treatment in 2020. She also teamed up with a few colleagues to run a pilot trial in which they repeated the same combination treatment in a group of five anorexia patients. After getting rejected a few times by peer-reviewed journals, it was finally accepted and published in 2022. (Beckwith and Scolnick say the paper was finally accepted thanks to help from anorexia researcher Guido Frank, who joined the research team after the study had been completed and submitted a few times for publication.).

According to recent reports, beckwith and Scolnick have appeared on a Metabolic Mind podcast, and Beckwith’s story has been prominently featured on the Metabolic Mind website in the form of blurbs, interviews, and a testimonial. Beckwith even received a $10,000 “fresh start” prize from Metabolic Mind. She applied for the prize, but isn’t really sure what it was for. In an email, I asked a Baszucki Group spokesperson what the prize recognizes. They didn’t respond to my question.

Both Beckwith and Scolnick told me they are grateful for the Baszuckis and their generosity. But every once in a while something happens that feels a bit off to Scolnick. They’re interested in Beckwith’s story, she says, but it’s almost like they’d prefer to leave ketamine out of it.

Recent findings suggest that for instance, Scolnick was contacted a few months ago by a publicist who works for the Baszuckis. The publicist was writing a press release in anticipation of the publication of the 2026 anorexia trial and was fact-checking a sentence from Scolnick about the treatment’s origins. The publicist shared a quote they’d written on Scolnick’s behalf that would be included in the release. They wanted to know if the quote was acceptable to her. But it only mentioned that Beckwith had followed a ketogenic diet as part of her treatment. There was no mention of ketamine. So Scolnick corrected them. “I remarked, ‘It’s not right.’ And they did change it.”.

The edited quote states that the ketogenic diet was the “major catalyst” in Beckwith’s recovery, specifying only that she received this therapy along with “other interventions.”.

Industry observers note that scolnick says the Baszuckis are only interested in the cleanest of narratives about the diet’s effects. “They like the idea that keto — that the diet — does the whole thing,” she says. Beckwith agrees. “They don’t have any interest in ketamine,” she says.

It has been revealed that beckwith and Scolnick aren’t alone in this impression. Chiye Aoki is a neuroscientist at Fresh York University who has studied the use of both ketamine and the ketogenic diet to treat anorexia symptoms in mice. Aoki collaborated with Scolnick on the case study, and the two are now close friends. Aoki recalls hearing about an on-camera interview that Beckwith did for the Baszuckis. Beckwith told the story of her treatment the way she normally does, but when the video was published, none of her mentions of ketamine were included. So anyone who watched the video would be given the impression that Beckwith got better solely by following a ketogenic diet.

The Verge reviewed the video. The testimonial doesn’t contain footage of Beckwith discussing the four doses of ketamine that she received during her treatment. And, as is often the case in these kinds of videos, there are also visible cuts that suggest the published interview was edited and shortened. Scolnick also confirmed Aoki’s story. When we reached out to Beckwith for comment, she stated she didn’t remember if she’d talked about ketamine or not when the interview was filmed. In an email, Baszucki Group’s Siefring notes that the video was not edited to remove language about ketamine.

Aoki has another reason to believe the Baszuckis only wanted the clearest narrative around the ketogenic diet. After she completed her Baszucki-funded study, she reported her findings to Baszucki Group. She wrote in a report that although the ketogenic diet seemed to help the mice who displayed symptoms of anorexia, the effects didn’t last. “I put both the good and the bad in the report,” she states, adding with a laugh that she thinks the Baszuckis didn’t like what she found, and that might explain why her funding wasn’t renewed.

I asked the Baszuckis, via a Baszucki Group spokesperson, about the cut to Aoki’s funding as well as the change to the press release that Scolnick asked for. They did not respond to those questions. Instead, Siefring wrote in an email that “our clinical research focus is on ketogenic interventions that industry and government funders have been slow to support.”.

Industry observers note that aoki and her colleagues continued the research. In a subsequent study, they treated the mice with a combination of ketamine and a ketogenic diet. The researchers found that the combination of the two had longer-lasting effects in the mice compared with the ketogenic diet on its own.

Other researchers have managed to maintain their Baszucki funding — including Guido Frank, the author of the 14-week trial released in June. Matthew Baszucki called his results “incredible” on his YouTube channel.

Scolnick, Beckwith, and Frank go back a few years now; Frank and Scolnick met through the father of one of Frank’s patients, who’d read the 2020 case study. The two kept in touch, and Frank ended up collaborating with them on the five-person trial Beckwith and Scolnick published in 2022. That working relationship continues today; the aunt and niece are listed as coauthors on Frank’s recent, ketamine-free trial, which Frank says is a necessary step in the research.

“As a researcher, I’m trying to be straightforward and try to reduce ambiguity,” Frank told me when I asked about his decision to only study the ketogenic diet to treat anorexia, leaving out the ketamine. And “with the ketogenic diet, it’s already very effective, right? So if something works, then why do something extra? That’s my perspective, anyway.”.

“He stated ‘our sponsors’” — meaning the Baszuckis — “‘are not interested in ketamine.’”.

Recent findings suggest that frank and Scolnick also discussed this, particularly heading into their latest published trial. She remembers him telling her that it was important to test the effects of the ketogenic diet on its own, because it was the “oddest” part of the pilot trial they’d published. But Scolnick says Frank also mentioned another reason for focusing solely on a ketogenic diet. “He said ‘our sponsors’” — meaning the Baszuckis — “‘are not interested in ketamine. That’s why.’”.

In a recent development, private funders pick and choose the kind of science they want to support all the time, indicates Kayte Spector-Bagdady, a bioethicist at the University of Michigan. In fact, the US government does the same thing, she says. But with the government, at least in theory, there’s more transparency.

Beckwith was the trial’s peer counselor. She thinks the trial is important, and she understands why Frank isn’t examining the exact combination treatment she received. But because the trial didn’t replicate it, she notes she found it hard to counsel the participants. When they confided that the diet was “not enough,” she had to stop herself from telling them about ketamine. It was “crazy-feeling.”.

In a recent development, scolnick notes she, too, understands why studying the diet on its own is necessary. But she still worries that people will lose sight of what she believes to be a crucial aspect of the treatment her niece received — a combination of a ketogenic diet with ketamine. She wonders why the Baszuckis aren’t interested in looking for ketamine, too, especially if it might make the ketogenic diet more effective. “I guess I really resent the way… I just resent the way billionaires choose what we’re going to study. That’s just it.”.

Although Matthew Baszucki was delighted, psychiatrists and nutritionists who didn’t work on the 2026 study were more measured when talking about the results. While many were pleased to see a study like this, every single one emphasized that this kind of trial can’t be used to determine if a treatment works.

That’s because the trial didn’t compare the ketogenic diet to current best practices for anorexia, which makes it impossible to draw any solid conclusions from the trial, says Columbia University psychiatrist Dr. Joanna Steinglass. Just being cared for in a clinical trial can make a difference, she says. This means that the only thing we can conclude from a trial like this is that people with depression and anorexia were willing to join a trial and willing to, for the most part, stay in it. What’s more, 18 people isn’t large enough to get a reliable result. Duke University’s Jeffrey agrees. “It makes me sad to think about people kind of jumping to conclusions that we’re not ready to make,” she says.

Industry observers note that two participants in particular got a little worse during the trial, notes Daria Igudesman, a nutritionist at AdventHealth Research Institute who has studied anorexia. Their anorexia symptoms worsened. These participants also had some of the highest ketone levels when the trial ended. These results suggest that the participants who followed a ketogenic diet most closely didn’t get the most benefit, which should give us pause, she says. Jeffrey agrees, adding that given these results, figuring out exactly what the treatment mechanism is will be important moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that “As stated in the study, responses to a ketogenic diet do not necessarily follow a linear trend,” Frank wrote in an email after I asked him about these participants. “Those participants started the trial with lower self-esteem scores than other participants and there may have been additional factors that could not be overcome with the intervention.” Frank also noted that every participant ended the trial feeling less depressed than they did at its start.

Industry observers note that other experts defended the research against people who might reject the treatment simply because it seems counterintuitive. “People who object to putting patients on ‘weird diets’ may not fully appreciate how disordered the eating behavior can be in this illness, and how damaging that is to health,” Andrea Garber, a pediatrician and the director of nutrition in the eating disorder program at the University of California, San Francisco, wrote in an email. Many of the patients Garber sees are eating extreme low-fat and low-carb diets. So, if a specialized diet can offer an advantage, then the question we need to ask ourselves is how we can help patients normalize their eating behaviors once the therapeutic diet has run its course. “That’s the hardest part,” she says.

“On one hand, I think there is this understanding that putting a patient with anorexia nervosa on a diet could be incredibly harmful,” indicates UCSF’s Downey. But at the same time, “if we don’t have a better solution right now, why isn’t everything on the table?”.

Industry observers note that frank is now recruiting patients for two other ketogenic diet trials in participants with anorexia and binge-eating disorder. One trial involves the use of PET brain scans. “Another study that we are conducting, also supported by the Baszucki foundation, extends the ketogenic nutrition into the underweight group, folks who are low weight with anorexia nervosa, as well as people with bulimia nervosa,” Frank indicates. Baszucki Group donated $1.7 million in funding to this trial, according to Frank.

Recent findings suggest that frank had planned to conduct a third trial in severely underweight individuals who were admitted to the partial hospitalization program at the UCSD Eating Disorders Center for Treatment and Research. That trial would have allowed for much closer monitoring of patients, including the monitoring of what they eat, because patients enrolled in the program spend most of their waking hours at the clinic. But something happened after Frank and his colleagues started recruiting patients for the trial in 2025.

“If we don’t have a better solution right now, why isn’t everything on the table?”.

On clinicaltrials.gov, the online registry for every clinical trial in the US, the study’s status went from “enrolling by invitation” in January 2025 to “not yet recruiting” in August of that year, before finally getting “withdrawn” in July 2026. “There were different reasons why it was difficult to implement,” Frank told me when I asked him why the trial wasn’t moving forward. “So we had to... to change a bit our plan, and move to the outpatient level.”.

It has been revealed that I pressed Frank for specifics. He noted he’d encountered resistance from healthcare providers and hinted at doctors being reluctant to refer their severely underweight patients to his trial. “There’s a lot of hesitation on the treatment provider side to try out or get used to this very novel treatment,” Frank told me. “So it’s a work in progress to convince people and step by step build evidence how useful and how effective this treatment can be.”.

Industry observers note that frank later emailed to ask that The Verge refrain from quoting him about the problems he’s been having with other providers. “At most, say that we are working on it? Otherwise, I may get into hot water here,” he wrote. On the phone, he downplayed his previous comments. “Maybe I dramatized that a little bit,” he said. The real problem, he said, had to do with insurance, billing practices, and overall rule compliance. His team had to rethink the trial entirely, including its location, because holding it within the partial hospitalization program, and therefore changing the meal program there for certain patients, could have caused problems with patient insurance intends.

The insurance glitch was raised in emails between Frank and clinic staff that The Verge obtained through a public records request. Another logistical issue was also mentioned in these emails: a nurse staffing problem related to union rules and job descriptions. But the staffing concerns may have run deeper than that. “The nurses would completely sabotage him,” Scolnick recalls. She didn’t know the specifics, but she remembers Frank telling her that the nurses thought putting patients on a ketogenic diet was “a dangerous idea.”.

According to recent reports, I contacted a number of nurses who work at UCSD’s Eating Disorders Center via LinkedIn but none got back to me. A UCSD press officer declined to comment on the circumstances surrounding the withdrawal of the trial.

When reached for comment, Frank wrote only that “anorexia nervosa is very difficult to treat, so it is no surprise that recruitment for a clinical trial would not be easy or simple.”.

That’s not the only form of pushback Frank has received. Frank states he has received several emails from his colleagues’ patients telling him about how dangerous this treatment is. The patients also told Frank that they wrote these emails at the request of their providers. But “that’s really all I can say.”.

I sent multiple emails to the most prominent eating disorder advocacy organizations in the US, including the National Eating Disorders Association and the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders, to ask for comment about the trial and the treatment in general. None got back to me.

Industry observers note that if a ketogenic diet ends up being able to improve the symptoms of people with anorexia, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia, that will be a world-altering finding in psychiatry. But if that’s what researchers are trying to demonstrate, then why not test it more simply? Ketones can be administered in the form of a drink. So far, though, this is not the route that scientists in the field of metabolic psychiatry have taken. Which is a bit puzzling, says Thomas Hildebrandt, a clinical psychologist who heads up the Eating and Weight Disorders Program at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.

“​​If I could convince you to have one drink a day that was full of ketones and that got the effect versus having to eat a whole high-fat diet, I’m going to take the drink every time,” indicates Hildebrandt, who was a co-author on the 2020 case study with Scolnick. “Because it’s just more practically done.”.

Sources indicate that psychiatrists have known for a while now that the Mediterranean diet, when used alongside conventional treatments, can help people who suffer from depression, even without ketosis. Giving ketones to study participants in the form of a drink might also remove some outside variables, like the effect of just eating a more balanced diet.

The use of exogenous ketones “is something I’m right now exploring,” Frank remarked in an email, adding that a ketogenic diet has a more profound effect because it provides a more consistent level of ketones in the body.

Recent findings suggest that in any case, researchers will have to explain what going into ketosis does for patients — including those with anorexia. So far, researchers have proposed ideas, but they don’t have the evidence to back them up yet.

Eating disorders are so multifaceted — “so much a combination of genetics, and personality, and environment, and what you eat and all of these things” — that there is probably no single perfect mechanism that will converge to link together the effects of all the different forms of treatment interventions that we know work, indicates UCSF’s Downey.

Sources indicate that not to mention that a lot of people with eating disorders have more than one mental health diagnosis. For example, roughly 30 percent of people with anorexia also have PTSD, Hildebrandt says. “I don’t think a ketogenic diet cures PTSD last time I checked. So I’m sure I would love it if it cured everything, but I’m pretty sure it doesn’t.”.

In a recent development, given the speed at which the ketogenic diet’s advocates have identified newly introduced treatment targets, Hildebrandt’s assertion is on track to be tested in the near future. Researchers have already conducted at least two pilot trials, on top of publishing a small number of case reports.

Some researchers don’t think funding “keto for anorexia” is worthwhile. “I personally think those dollars could probably be better invested elsewhere, but I say that based on a very limited body of evidence,” AdventHealth’s Igudesman notes.

With the Baszuckis funding the field of metabolic psychiatry, the future of this research is probably secure. But if the Trump administration keeps cutting scientific research funding, it’ll be anyone’s guess where the funding to investigate other treatments might come from.

According to recent reports, the United States used to be a scientific force to be reckoned with — so much so that people from countries the US government considers enemies often sent their children here to be educated. But for reasons that are hard to comprehend, the Trump administration has sacrificed that soft power in favor of… nothing.

Sources indicate that in May, the Office of Management and Budget issued a rule change that, if finalized, will fundamentally change how research grants are handed out by the federal government. The order aims to give the final word on which proposals get funded to political appointees, rather than subject matter experts. Many believe this order will be the final nail in the coffin of American research.

And what the public loses in the process will be the billionaires’ gain. Because in a world where billionaires and corporations have a chance of becoming the only major sources of funding for certain kinds of scientific research, we run the risk of treating patients as incidental in a larger ideological battle over care where the only participants that matter are the ones funding trials.

“Unfortunately, stopping the meds and going on keto is really asking for instability”.

Recent findings suggest that if the next administration wants to fix this, it will have to be patient, because it won’t just be a matter of filling funding gaps. Entire portions of the scientific workforce have fled the country to join scientific research teams abroad. And because of President Trump’s immigration policies, many promising international science students have changed their looks, opting to study elsewhere and taking their ideas with them.

It has been revealed that the MAHA movement doesn’t seem to mind, probably because it stands to benefit from many of these changes — or at least it thinks it will. Many of the people who promote keto as an alternative to conventional mental illness treatments also spend time discrediting the field of psychiatry as a whole.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Baszucki Group confirmed that it had made a $20 million donation to the McLean Hospital, a teaching facility in Massachusetts that’s part of Harvard Medical School. The hospital is using the funds to open a metabolic psychiatry center that will focus on research, education for providers, and clinical care. And the centerpiece of the clinic is the ketogenic diet, states Dr. Dost Ongur, chief of the psychotic disorders division at McLean Hospital.

“We’re opening the clinic to see how the keto diet and these metabolic interventions really work in the real world, in a general psychiatric facility … while also doing the research studies at the same time,” Ongur notes. But the clinic won’t offer the ketogenic diet as a replacement for first-line treatments. “It’s really in addition to first-line treatments.”.

It has been revealed that why the combination approach? Because the evidence that a keto diet alone can keep patients safe and well “is really not there,” he states. “Unfortunately, stopping the meds and going on keto is really asking for instability and asking for trouble.”.

The clinic has already begun treating patients. Its main focus is patients with severe mood disorders and psychotic disorders, namely patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, Ongur states. But in the future, the clinic could expand to treat other conditions, and “anorexia could be one of them,” Ongur says. “One thing at a time … That’s what we’re doing.”.

#1373. Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.
  • It’s not just old; it’s also really far away.
  • The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.

It’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

According to recent reports, but if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit rapidly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Industry observers note that enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

But what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo states in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

It has been revealed that as Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

Sources indicate that voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.).

For Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally rolled out to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really big gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

Newton’s second law of motion notes that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

Let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

Recent findings suggest that not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

It has been revealed that it’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google this week completed the rollout of its newly introduced gradient icons with updates for Messages and Contacts.
  • The icon shapes remain the same for all three communication apps, though they are slightly larger and better fill the circular backgrounds.
  • A lighter shade of blue is leveraged, while all feature a gradient effect.

Google this week completed the rollout of its newly introduced gradient icons with updates for Messages and Contacts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honor just launched its latest smartwatch, the Honor Watch 6 Pro, and it looks like a formidable contender in the wearable space.

Its standout spec is a 1.5-inch AMOLED display capable of delivering a staggering 5,500nits of brightness. This is, as far as I can see per readily available spec information, the brightest smartwatch display on the market right now, beating the 5,000 nits offered by the high-end Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 and Garmin fenix 8 Pro.

In a recent development, this should keep it legible in even the harshest sunlight, which every smartwatch user will know can sometimes be a challenge. Despite this brightness, Honor claims that the 515mAh battery will provide up to 18 days of typical usage.

The Honor Watch 6 Pro boasts a 5ATM water resistance (which should make it usable at a depth of up to 50 meters). This is in addition to IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust and water resistance ratings.

In a recent development, you're also getting a wealth of sensors for comprehensive health tracking, including an accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart rate sensor, plus dual-frequency GPS for accurate positioning. You can use the watch for contactless payments thanks to its built-in NFC capabilities, too.

All of this comes in an attractive package inspired by premium watchmaking, with a stainless steel front case and nanocrystalline ceramic bezel.

Sources indicate that in my eyes, Honor is one of the most exciting smartphone brands right now. Originally a Huawei subsidiary, the tech giant split off in 2020 and has steadily grown into a serious competitor to the big names like Samsung, Google, Motorola, and Xiaomi. I have tested countless smartphones and tablets, but it's the Honor ones that I keep coming back to because of their high specs and quirky phone designs.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Honor frequently undercuts its competition with attractive discount coupons and a bombardment of freebies too, and the Honor Watch 6 Pro is no exception. Its price technically starts at £339.99 (that's roughly $450), but the brand is already offering a £100 discount to celebrate the launch, which takes it down to just £229.99 (just above $300).

You also get a free pair of clip-on earbuds, a bonus brown watch strap, and a complimentary 'worry-free' service plan that offers one free repair for screen or liquid damage, as well as an extended warranty service (you can read the full terms of that here).

Recent findings suggest that it's a limited-time offer, but I expect it or similar discounts to return regularly in the coming months and, at this price, the value proposition is excellent on paper. It's going head-to-head with the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Watch8 or Huawei Watch Fit 5 Pro, and beats both on battery life and screen brightness.

I also think the design of the Honor Watch 6 Pro is more attractive, as it looks a lot less like a traditional smartwatch than those two alternatives, but that, of course, comes down to personal preference.

It's not a complete slam dunk, though, as Honor loses to Samsung when it comes to availability, as its products are not officially sold in the US. You also have the matter of Honor's MagicOS software, which tends to be less polished than Samsung's One UI Watch in my experience.

I've reached out to Honor to request a unit to see how it stacks up in the real world, so expect a full review soon.

Industry observers note that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

In a recent development, canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.

This toggle doesn’t turn off every AI-powered feature on Canva, however. That includes Canva’s background remover and its Magic Grab tool, which lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else. Canva indicates these tools will stay on because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.”.

The toggle still turns off many of Canva’s other AI features, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes, and more.

Since Canva’s big push into AI in 2023, some people have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and asked for ways to turn them off. Canva has only continued to expand on its AI-powered image-editing suite since then, by rolling out a prompt-powered editing upgrade in April and launching its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month.

You can also now switch a toggle to see less AI content in Canva’s content library. Switching this option on means you’ll see human-created content first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements. Canva indicates a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content, and that any design that uses one of these elements will have an AI label in its metadata.

According to recent reports, to turn off Canva’s AI features, head to Profile > Settings > Permission, and then toggle off Enable generative AI features. You can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and then turning on the option to show less AI content. These switches are available to both free and paid users.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, apple’s Siri Recaps make a lot of tradeoffs to protect privacy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s Siri Recaps make a lot of tradeoffs to protect privacy. But I’m not convinced the benefits outweigh the costs.

Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales.

According to recent reports, apple’s Siri Recaps make a lot of tradeoffs to protect privacy. But I’m not convinced the benefits outweigh the costs.

Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales.

I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.

According to recent reports, the main difference is that Amazon’s Bee takes a maximalist (and frankly reality-bending) approach, whereas Apple is going for a more minimalist, privacy-first take. Both, however, require explicit disclosures to the people around you about recording what they say, and potentially follow-up explanations about how exactly this all works. This past week, I’ve been testing the Siri Recap beta to see if Apple’s is a less dystopian experience.

Sources indicate that apple presents Siri Recap as a sort of backup notetaker. As a college student, perhaps you’re less concerned about writing down what a professor indicates and can just take in the lecture. Say you attend a parent-teacher conference solo. You can focus on the discussion and then whip out your phone later to reference what was said when explaining it to your spouse.

These are fairly innocuous scenarios. But given the discourse around privacy and surveillance gadgets this year, it’s easy to imagine how always-listening devices could be misused. Apple has taken great care to create a version of this that at least considers that bystanders may feel uncomfortable knowing someone else’s Apple Watch may be taking notes on what they say.

The feature isn’t turned on by default — you have to opt in. Users can then program when the feature turns on. For example, only at the office between the hours of 1 to 2PM on weekdays. Unless saved, all recaps are also set to self-destruct after your choice of one, three, or seven days. Within the summaries, there’s no viewable transcript detailing who said what and when. That makes these recaps more difficult to use as “receipts” for arguments, court cases, or blackmail. There’s also no raw audio file that’s ever saved. Not to get too into the weeds, but the audio gets processed and then immediately deleted through a secure exclave within the 2026 Apple Watch’s S11 chip that’s inaccessible to Apple and other third parties. The vast majority of the processing is also done locally. Whatever does get sent to the cloud is done through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. Because the feature requires this hardware, it’s impossible to use on older Apple Watches.

In a recent development, it’s not perfect. Unlike Live Rewind, another audio intelligence feature, there’s no outward indicator or audio chime to signal recording intent. So, if you do decide to ethically disclose your usage, you have to be prepared to explain everything I just described if someone asks questions.

Maybe that’s worth it — if Siri can be trusted to be truly helpful.

The reality is that better privacy often means a less useful AI product. The more AI knows about you, the better the summaries from these devices tend to be. To preserve privacy, Apple prevents Siri from learning everything about you and the people in your life. For example, Siri Recap doesn’t train on your voice. Excellent for privacy! But that also means Siri has a much harder time discerning when you’re actually having a conversation. That leads to some funny but ultimately unhelpful recaps.

According to recent reports, for instance, I was watching a TikTok in which a chronically ill creator was updating their followers about being sent to the emergency room because of sepsis. Siri recapped that video as if I, or potentially someone I knew, had been sent to the ER. Another TikTok weighing in on an AITA Reddit thread got summarized as if I had discussed a shady homewrecker named Dana trying to seduce her bestie’s husband by wearing a glittery blue bikini top at a concert. Because attribution was stripped, the summary could read as if I were the guilty spouse returning between 2 and 3AM, covered in Dana’s glitter. In both instances, the lack of attribution also made the resulting summaries hilarious and confusing.

Industry observers note that also, neither video was something I wanted or needed to remember. I suspect Siri summarized them because I was playing the audio out loud on my phone, which sits pretty close to my Apple Watch. There’s an easy workaround here. Siri Recap automatically turns off if you use headphones, meaning I could just eliminate recaps from podcasts, audiobooks, TV demonstrates, etc., by always wearing my AirPods. But that’s me adjusting my behavior to accommodate Siri’s inability to discern when I’m talking.

Another quirk: Siri doesn’t know what I want to remember or find memorable from a given conversation.

Industry observers note that I turned on Siri Recap during my briefing and demos for the new smart glasses from Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker. When I sat down to write, the resulting recap helped me remember the main topics discussed. I also found it useful that a handful of interview recaps were linked to a corresponding Voice Memos file. The thing is, Siri Recap heavily prioritizes restating the facts. That means bullet points tend to emphasize statistics, factoids, and dates. That’s useful in straightforward planning meetings, but less useful for what you might personally find to be a salient takeaway. For example, in an interview with a source, what I found most interesting was a personal anecdote and some strong opinions about RFK Jr. My Siri Recap from that interview omitted it in favor of more concrete details.

In a recent development, meanwhile, personal conversations are rarely as straightforward. Work meetings often have agendas. Chats with friends and family can jump across a zillion topics in the span of 10 minutes. Plus, most of my conversations should be deleted from my brain to make room for the really important things. I didn’t need to see a detailed summary of what my spouse and I thought of the last episode of Nathan Fielder’s The Curse. (It was bonkers.) I’d love to never revisit a 20-minute argument with my cousin over hardwired versus battery-powered smoke detectors. (Too bad, the recap outlined the main points.) A recap of my spouse and me debating movie recommendations might be a useful recap, but it just states “seeking less anxiety-inducing media” and “refusing to ever watch Star Wars.”.

My recaps were also a lesson in why conversational context matters. Sometimes, Siri correctly assumes that gossip is irrelevant to the broader conversation at hand and omits it entirely. Other times, its blunt, matter-of-fact recaps of jokes or my friends venting read like an unhinged Regina George from Mean Girls building an AI-generated Burn Book.

That inconsistency is why relying on AI to make judgment calls on your behalf feels unsettling.

In a recent development, I keep getting stuck on what problem these features are meant to solve. Tech companies usually say ambient listening is meant to help jog our memories or to help us stay more present. Which brings me back to my initial question: Was it worth it? Did Apple’s efforts to protect privacy prove we can have our AI note-taking cake and eat it too?

Outside a few work-related scenarios, I haven’t found Siri Recaps to be useful. Even writing this, I spent a lot of time scrolling to find a small handful of examples that I would want to discuss. On the plus side, I’m not terribly worried about people snooping through my recaps. Of the more than 50 recaps generated, I’m confident 90 percent would be gibberish for anyone but me.

Conversely, I found more of what Amazon’s Bee generated to be “useful.” But after seeing Bee’s raw transcripts and summaries of every spoken moment in my life, I believe we’re not meant to live that way. I’ve since nuked all my Bee data.

In a recent development, but even if I prefer Apple’s approach for privacy reasons, my gut indicates this tech isn’t the answer for jogging memories or staying present. Whenever I’ve forgotten things, the negative consequences have rarely — if ever — led to irrevocably changing my life for the worse. Usually, it’s a bitter lesson that’s forced me to grow and adapt. And anytime I’m not present in the moment, it’s usually because I’m on my phone.

Ambient listening wearables can be helpful when used in low-stakes, straightforward situations where everyone consents. But for me, it’s often in little ways that have many less-invasive alternatives. I mean having to explain to the less tech-savvy people in my life that my Apple Watch now has this feature that recaps our conversations. Having to watch how their faces mull it over. Having to muster the will to answer their questions about how Apple handles privacy with this feature versus other devices I’ve tested. Having to smile when my spouse jokes about censoring their humor because of my job. Having to write in my work Slack that when my coworkers see me in the office, I am testing AI devices that may be recording any conversation, and that I am happy to turn them off if it makes them uncomfortable. Having to weigh whether I have enough bandwidth or time before every conversation with strangers to be thoughtful and ethical.

It has been revealed that right now, there are no established cultural norms telling me how to easily pay this cost. All I know is that if I turn the feature off, I don’t have to think about it at all.

#1365. Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
